overview: Everest Group, Ltd. is a Bermuda-domiciled global reinsurance and insurance holding company (formerly Everest Re Group, renamed 2023) that has written P&C business since 1973. The company underwrites property, casualty and specialty reinsurance (catastrophe, mortgage, marine, aviation, engineering, professional lines, credit/surety, motor, agriculture/crop, political violence) alongside a shrinking book of specialty/wholesale primary insurance, operating through brokers, ceding companies, wholesale/retail/surplus-lines channels and program administrators across the US, Europe, Bermuda and internationally. Following the 2025 sale of most global retail commercial insurance renewal rights to AIG and a 2026 wave of further retail-insurance divestitures (Canada to Wawanesa, Colombia and Chile to AIG, Mexico to Fairfax), Everest now reports three segments: Reinsurance Treaty, Global Wholesale & Specialty, and Legacy, and is substantially complete in its pivot away from primary retail insurance back toward a reinsurance/specialty-led model.

business_model.summary: Everest earns underwriting profit (premiums less losses and expenses) plus float income from investing premiums before claims are paid. Reinsurance (treaty and facultative) is the larger, higher-margin engine; the much-reduced primary/specialty insurance book has been the source of recurring reserve trouble. A large ($40B+) fixed-income-heavy investment portfolio generates substantial and growing net investment income (record quarterly NII of $634M in Q3 2026) that has become an increasingly important earnings driver, now cushioning underwriting-side losses from catastrophes and casualty reserve strengthening.
business_model.customer_type: B2B — ceding insurance companies and reinsurance brokers (Reinsurance segment); wholesale/retail brokers, surplus lines brokers and program administrators (Insurance segment)
business_model.geographic_mix: US, Bermuda, Europe (Ireland/UK hubs), and international operations; FY2025 gross written premium of $17.7B, split roughly 72% Reinsurance / 27% Insurance, with the Insurance segment's geographic footprint narrowing further in 2026 as Canada, Colombia, Chile and (pending) Mexico retail units are sold off

competitive_position.market_position: Top-tier global reinsurer by premium volume, now re-concentrating around a reinsurance/specialty-led model after largely exiting primary retail commercial insurance through 2025-2026; management is deliberately shrinking US casualty reinsurance volume (written premium down ~18% in Q3 2026) to prioritize underwriting discipline over growth amid a softening and more competitive market.

moat_factors.description: $17.7B FY2025 GWP across property, casualty, specialty and mortgage reinsurance lines provides diversification benefits and large-line capacity that smaller reinsurers cannot match

A+ (AM Best) / AA- (S&P) financial strength ratings support participation on large treaties and cat programs, though all three major agencies carry negative outlooks following repeated casualty reserve charges
Decades-long relationships with reinsurance brokers and ceding companies support renewal retention, though reinsurance is a largely commoditized, price-competitive market with low switching costs

$40B+ investment portfolio and growing alternative-asset/limited-partnership allocation generate a meaningful and growing float-income advantage, with record net investment income increasingly offsetting underwriting volatility

weaknesses: US casualty reserve inadequacy has now recurred for three consecutive years (2024-2026), with booked reserves reported over $850M above the actuarial central estimate as of Q3 2026, undermining underwriting credibility and triggering a securities-law investigation into prior disclosures
Reinsurance is a commoditized, cyclical market with limited pricing power versus peers in soft markets; property pricing has continued to soften through 2026

Primary insurance franchise has been almost entirely dismantled (AIG renewal-rights sale plus Canada/Colombia/Chile/Mexico divestitures), reducing diversification and scale in that segment and concentrating earnings in the more cyclical reinsurance business
Smaller and less specialized in property-catastrophe than RenaissanceRe, and less diversified than Berkshire/Munich Re/Swiss Re in non-P&C lines

Q3 2026 Reinsurance Treaty combined ratio deteriorated sharply (up 21.5 points YoY to 108.5%) on casualty reserve strengthening plus elevated catastrophe losses, producing a group-level pre-tax underwriting loss

growth_drivers: Global Wholesale & Specialty segment continuing to grow (GWP +3% in Q3 2026) and post profitable underwriting (97.3% combined ratio) as the core specialty growth engine

Continued growth in net investment income (record $634M in Q3 2026, up from $540M a year earlier) from portfolio growth, elevated reinvestment yields, and alternative/limited-partnership returns, increasingly offsetting underwriting-side volatility

Completion of the retail-insurance exit (AIG renewal rights, Canada to Wawanesa, Colombia/Chile to AIG, Mexico to Fairfax pending 2027 close) freeing capital and management attention for higher-return reinsurance/specialty underwriting

Large, ongoing share buyback program ($474M repurchased in Q3 2026 alone, part of $550M total capital returned that quarter) supporting per-share value growth, especially while the stock trades at a depressed multiple
Selective, disciplined capital deployment into international and specialty lines that management views as offering the most attractive risk-adjusted returns in the current cycle
Potential for a firmer casualty reinsurance pricing response industrywide as cedents and reinsurers alike reprice long-tail US liability risk following multi-year, sector-wide social-inflation losses

business.description: A third consecutive year of material adverse development: ~$600M gross casualty reserve strengthening in Q3 2026 (net adverse development of roughly $253-268M that quarter) followed over $200M in Q2 2026, on top of $1.7B in FY2025 and $1.3B in FY2024; management says booked reserves now sit over $850M above the actuarial central estimate, but further charges remain a live risk

Property reinsurance pricing has continued to soften through 2026 amid abundant traditional and alternative capital; management is deliberately cutting US casualty reinsurance volume (down ~18% in Q3 2026) rather than compete on price, pressuring top-line growth into 2027

business.risk: Shrunken, geographically fragmented primary insurance franchise
business.description: Sequential sales of retail commercial insurance units (AIG renewal rights, Canada, Colombia, Chile, pending Mexico) have left a much smaller, specialty-focused Insurance segment, concentrating the group's earnings in the more cyclical and currently loss-making Reinsurance Treaty segment

financial.description: Elevated catastrophe losses of $277M in Q3 2026 (versus $43M a year earlier), driven by the Colombia earthquake and Middle East events, illustrate continued exposure to sharp quarterly earnings swings from large natural and man-made events

$40B+ predominantly fixed-income portfolio is exposed to interest rate moves and credit spread widening; alternative/LP allocations add mark-to-market volatility even as they currently support record net investment income

financial.risk: Reserve charges eroding capital efficiency and net income
financial.description: Q3 2026 net income fell to $233M from $255M a year earlier (net operating income to $290M from $316M) despite record investment income, as repeated adverse development continues to depress ROE and underwriting profitability

regulatory.risk: Multi-jurisdictional regulatory/capital requirements and M&A approvals
regulatory.description: Bermuda-domiciled but subject to US, UK/EU (Solvency II-equivalent) and other regulatory capital regimes; the string of 2026 retail-insurance divestitures (Canada, Colombia, Chile, Mexico) each require separate regulatory approvals across jurisdictions, adding execution complexity and timing risk

AM Best, S&P and Moody's have all carried negative outlooks since October 2025 following reserve charges; continued casualty deterioration raises the risk of an actual downgrade that would raise cost of capital and could affect cedent/broker relationships

regulatory.risk: Securities litigation / regulatory scrutiny over reserve disclosures
regulatory.description: Law firms (e.g., Johnson Fistel) have announced investigations into whether Everest's financial disclosures around its casualty reserve charges violated federal securities laws, following sharp reserve-driven stock price declines in both late 2025 and 2026

macro.description: Elevated loss emergence in US excess casualty and liability lines driven by social inflation remains the central sector-wide trend pressuring Everest's and peers' reserves into 2027
Falling rates would reduce reinvestment yields on the large fixed-income book and slow net investment income growth, which has become a critical offset to weak underwriting results
Increasing frequency/severity of secondary perils and named catastrophes (e.g., the 2026 Colombia earthquake and Middle East events) raises modeled loss costs across the reinsurance industry

execution.description: Following CEO Juan Andrade's abrupt January 2025 resignation and Jim Williamson's confirmation as permanent CEO, Everest also transitioned CFOs in 2026 (Elias Habayeb replacing Mark Kociancic) alongside new group chief actuary and chief risk officer appointments — concentrated leadership turnover during an unresolved reserve-adequacy episode

Simultaneously closing/transitioning several retail-insurance sales (Canada, Colombia, Chile, pending Mexico) while re-underwriting the US casualty book and integrating new finance/actuarial leadership creates meaningful near-term operational complexity and distraction risk

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global reinsurance capacity remains ample (traditional + alternative/ILS capital); property-cat pricing continued to soften through 2026 after the 2023-2024 hard market, while US casualty/liability reserve risk (social inflation) remains the dominant sector-wide concern heading into 2027 renewals
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — reinsurance pricing and underwriting margins move through multi-year hard/soft cycles driven by catastrophe loss experience, capital flows and (for casualty) multi-year loss-emergence lags
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high — large fixed income portfolio; net investment income benefits from higher reinvestment yields and alternative-asset returns (record NII in 2026), but falling rates or credit spread widening would pressure both NII and portfolio marks
key_input_costs: Claims/loss cost inflation (social inflation, medical cost trend, litigation funding)

recent_developments.event: Q3 2025: Everest reported roughly $361-478M (sources vary) of prior-year US casualty reserve strengthening; shares fell over 11% on the day; AM Best, S&P and Moody's all moved to negative outlooks; Everest secured a $1.2B Adverse Development Cover on North America Insurance liabilities for accident years 2024 and prior
Everest announced sale of renewal rights to the majority of its global retail commercial insurance business (~$2B GWP) to AIG, covering US, UK, European and Asia-Pacific operations
Full-year 2025 results: $17.7B gross written premium, Group combined ratio 98.6%, net income $1.6B; FY2025 total adverse reserve development of $1.7B pre-tax

Everest agreed to sell Everest Insurance Company of Canada to Wawanesa for ~$410M; AM Best placed the unit's rating under review with negative implications pending close; deal completed October 1, 2026
Everest advanced its commercial-retail exit by agreeing to sell its Chile insurance operations to AIG, alongside completion of the previously announced Colombia sale to AIG

CFO transition announced: Elias Habayeb named incoming EVP and Group CFO (effective ~May 2026), succeeding Mark Kociancic; Katy Bradica named group chief actuary and Attila Kerényi named group chief risk officer in a broader C-suite refresh
Everest agreed to sell its Mexico insurance business to Fairfax Financial, with close expected in 2027, as part of completing the exit from remaining commercial retail insurance operations

Q2 2026 operating EPS of $14.85 beat consensus by ~1.8%; core businesses posted $317M underwriting income on a ~90% combined ratio; ~$200M of additional casualty reserve strengthening recorded; over $470M returned to shareholders

Q3 2026 results: revenue of $3.71B (down 14% YoY, missed estimates), adjusted EPS $7.62 (~4.4% below consensus); Group combined ratio around 105.8-107% (sources vary) with Reinsurance Treaty deteriorating to 108.5% (up 21.5 points YoY) and a pre-tax underwriting loss of ~$223M; ~$600M gross / ~$253-268M net adverse casualty reserve development, the third consecutive year of such charges; catastrophe losses of $277M (Colombia earthquake, Middle East events) versus $43M a year earlier; record net investment income of $634M; net income $233M (down from $255M); GWP down 15% to $3.7B as management deliberately cut US casualty reinsurance volume ~18%-25% depending on sub-line; nine-month net income nonetheless rose to $1.5B from $1.2B on investment income strength; $550M returned to shareholders including $474M of buybacks; stock reaction was mixed across sources (some report a modest post-earnings gain, others a steep single-day drop around the disclosure), and law firms (e.g., Johnson Fistel) announced securities-litigation investigations into Everest's reserve disclosures

guidance.as_of: Q3 2026 Earnings (reported late October 2026) and Q2 2026 Earnings

items.target: Mid-to-high 90s for the full year (prudently positioned at the high end after Q3)
items.vs_prior: maintained (though Q3 printed above the group's own expected range on a reported basis per some data; management described the attritional/ex-cat, ex-PYD run rate as within range)
items.notes: Management reiterated underwriting-quality focus; actual Q3 group combined ratio came in materially elevated (~97-107% depending on reported vs. core-business basis) due to catastrophe losses and casualty reserve strengthening

items.target: Continued deliberate reduction (down ~18-25% YoY in Q3 2026 across casualty XOL/pro-rata)
items.notes: CEO Jim Williamson described the Treaty team as 'navigating the market cycle with the highest level of discipline,' prioritizing selectivity and best-in-class clients over volume

items.target: Selective deployment concentrated in international and specialty lines
items.notes: CFO Elias Habayeb said the company intends to keep loss picks conservative while growing specialty lines where risk-adjusted returns are most attractive

items.target: Continued aggressive buybacks and dividends; share repurchases remain a 'top priority'
items.notes: $550M returned to shareholders in Q3 2026 ($474M buybacks); annualized total shareholder return of 14.2% for the quarter cited by management; quarterly dividend maintained

items.target: No explicit new charge guided; booked reserves held >$850M above actuarial central estimate as a buffer
items.vs_prior: maintained (elevated caution, third straight year of charges)
items.notes: Management frames the added buffer as reducing — not eliminating — the risk of further adverse development in US excess casualty/liability lines

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Jim Williamson continued to frame 2026 as a disciplined repositioning year: prioritizing underwriting quality and capital return over premium growth, deliberately shrinking US casualty reinsurance exposure, and completing the multi-year exit from retail commercial insurance (Canada, Colombia, Chile, pending Mexico) to concentrate the franchise in Reinsurance Treaty and Global Wholesale & Specialty. CFO Elias Habayeb emphasized conservative loss picks and a reserve buffer now running over $850M above the actuarial central estimate, while acknowledging that a third consecutive year of casualty reserve strengthening has drawn renewed rating-agency and investor scrutiny, including securities-law investigation activity following the Q3 2026 disclosure.

bull_case: Record and growing net investment income ($634M in Q3 2026) from a large, diversified portfolio is increasingly offsetting underwriting-side volatility and supported a 25% rise in nine-month net income despite a weak reserve-driven Q3

Management has substantially completed the multi-year pivot away from capital-intensive, historically troubled retail primary insurance (AIG, Wawanesa, Colombia/Chile/Mexico sales), concentrating the franchise in higher-return reinsurance and specialty lines

Aggressive, sustained capital return (quarterly buybacks of $400-500M+, dividends, ~14% annualized shareholder return cited by management) directly supports per-share value creation while the stock trades at a depressed multiple relative to book value

Deliberate, disciplined reduction of US casualty reinsurance volume (down ~18-25% in Q3 2026) suggests management is finally repricing/de-risking the segment that has driven three straight years of reserve charges, rather than chasing volume
Global Wholesale & Specialty continues to grow profitably (97.3% combined ratio, +3% GWP in Q3 2026), demonstrating the remaining specialty franchise can both grow and underwrite well
bear_case: Three consecutive years of material US casualty adverse reserve development (FY2024, FY2025, and again in Q2/Q3 2026) raise serious doubts about reserve adequacy and management's ability to accurately price long-tail casualty risk, even after an ADC and a reported $850M+ reserve buffer

Q3 2026 Reinsurance Treaty combined ratio deteriorated sharply to 108.5% (up 21.5 points YoY) with a group pre-tax underwriting loss, showing the core reinsurance engine — not just legacy insurance — is now also underwriting at a loss

All three major rating agencies carry negative outlooks following repeated reserve charges, and continued deterioration raises real downgrade risk that would increase Everest's cost of capital and could impair cedent/broker relationships
Securities-law investigations/litigation stemming from reserve disclosures add legal, reputational and potential financial overhang on top of the underlying reserve problem

Years of sequential retail-insurance divestitures (US to AIG, Canada to Wawanesa, Colombia/Chile to AIG, Mexico to Fairfax) and simultaneous CFO/chief actuary/chief risk officer turnover signal a business still mid-restructuring, with execution and key-person risk elevated at a time investor confidence is already fragile

Deliberately shrinking premium volume (GWP down 15% in Q3 2026) in a softening pricing market means top-line contraction is likely to persist into 2027, placing the earnings growth story almost entirely on investment income and capital return rather than underwriting
